title: Halal and haram
hookLine: permitted and forbidden, with most of life in the wide permitted middle

lines: THE WORD ON THE BUTCHER'S WINDOW.
cards: You've seen the word on a butcher's window, a food truck, a candy wrapper. Halal. If you only know it from signs, you might picture Islam as one long list of don'ts.
No pork. No alcohol. No this, no that.

People new to the faith sometimes feel it too: a nervous sense that every choice is a test and every snack a trap. This week looks at halal plainly, and the first thing to know is where the weight actually sits.

teach.b: Arabic dictionaries, like Lane's, tie halal to a root meaning to untie, to release. What's halal has been let loose, made free for you.
Haram comes from a root meaning set apart, protected, the same root as al-Haram, the sanctuary in Mecca. Something haram is fenced off. Between the two lies nearly everything.

Islamic law sorts actions into five grades: required, recommended, simply permitted, disliked, and forbidden. The simply permitted, mubah, is enormous: walking, laughing, most food, most work, a nap, a joke.
And the law books state a principle for everyday things: the starting point is permission. You don't need a verse to allow a mango. You'd need one to forbid it.
Surah al-Baqarah says: He it is Who created for you all that is in the earth. For you. And a report in Tirmidhi says that what Allah is silent about, He has pardoned.
Sahih al-Bukhari tells of people who went the other way. Three men asked about the Prophet's worship and decided they had to outdo it. One would pray all night, every night.
One would fast every day. One would never marry. When the Prophet ﷺ heard, he said: I fast, and I eat.
I pray, and I sleep. I marry. And whoever turns away from my way is not of me.
The forbidden list is real, but it's short.

teach.h: A SMALL FENCE, AN OPEN LAND.
teach.b: The fence is around a small field. The rest of the land is open.

how: Muslims sort actions into required, recommended, permitted, disliked and forbidden, treating most everyday things as permitted unless a clear text forbids them.

o: meat from an animal raised outdoors
permitted, let loose for you to enjoy
food blessed by a prayer from an imam

games.q: what's inside halal and haram — tap the pairs.
p: from a root meaning to untie
tried to outdo the Prophet's worship

s: for everyday things, the law books say the starting point is permission
you'd need a text to forbid a mango, not to allow it.
haram and the Haram in Mecca share a root
both come from a root meaning set apart, protected.
the Prophet ﷺ praised the man who planned to fast every day
he said: I fast and I eat, I pray and I sleep, I marry (Bukhari).

games.q: three men decide to outdo the Prophet ﷺ: pray all night, fast every day, never marry. he hears about it. what does he say?
o: I fast and I eat, I pray and I sleep, I marry
only one of you may do it
games.why: he said whoever turns away from his way is not of him (Bukhari 5063). the permitted middle is part of the way, not a weakness.

practice: Name, slowly, five good things in your life that no one anywhere would call forbidden: a hot shower, your kid's laugh, the first sip of coffee, a walk, a friend's voice.

Count them on your fingers, and let each one land for a breath. If you pray, you can say alhamdulillah after each; if not, just notice how wide that open land is, and how much of your day it already covers.

wordCard.voice: Halal. Permitted, released, let loose: the wide open middle of life, with the forbidden fenced off at the edges. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: permitted, from the root h-l-l, to untie or release.

carryVoice: Your line: most things are allowed. A small choice doesn't have to be a trap. See you tomorrow.
